June 15, 2026 
 
Dr. Mehmet Oz 
Administrator 
Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services 
U.S. Department of Health and Human Services 
 
RE: CMS-0062-P – Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs 
 
Dear Administrator Oz, 
 
Physicians of Southwest Washington (PSW) and MultiCare Connected Care (MCC) are 
Clinically Integrated Networks (CINs) located in Washington State serving over 400,000 
individuals across the Pacific Northwest. These networks consist of numerous independent 
practices, health systems, and rural health systems that have joined together to find a better way 
to provide coordinated care for their patients.  
 
On behalf of PSW and MCC, we appreciate the opportunity to comment on the Interoperability 
Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs proposed rule issued on April 10. 
 
We support this rule and agree that it has the potential to reduce administrative burden over time 
and improve patient access to needed therapies. However, in its current form, the rule also 
presents significant operational, technical, and financial risks for organizations operating in 
delegated, value-based, and health plan-aligned models in the near term, particularly related to 
implementation complexity, multi-payer variation, and misalignment between accountability and 
operational control. We request that CMS address these impacts to ensure the proposed policy 
succeeds in practice. 
 
Summary 
 
Summary of Recommendations 
• Recognize and address the operational and IT burden created for delegated entities, CINs, 
Independent Provider Associations (IPAs), and other risk-bearing organizations, and 
ensure accountability aligns with control. 
• Require end-to-end, integrated workflows across all actors. 
• Standardize data elements and behavior across payers and lines of business. 
• Pair shorter timelines with safeguards and clear denial rationale. 
• Adopt phased implementation aligned to real-world operations. 
• Allow evolution of prior authorization in risk-bearing arrangements. 
 
 
 
 
 
1300 S Evergreen Park Dr SW, Suite 200, Olympia, WA 98502 | 360.943.4337 | 1.877.943.4337 | pswipa.com 
Detailed Recommendations 
 
Impact of Electronic Prior Authorization on Delegated Models 
We support end-to-end electronic prior authorization for prescription drugs. When supported by 
standardized data and reliable transaction performance, electronic prior authorization can reduce 
avoidable delays, manual rework and duplicate submissions; help patients access high-cost 
therapies more quickly; and improve visibility into coverage requirements, documentation needs, 
and status across the authorization process. 
 
While this proposed rule regulates payers, it will also have significant downstream impacts on 
delegated entities, CINs, IPAs, and other organizations operating between traditional payer and 
provider roles. In these models, organizations may be accountable for authorization performance, 
care coordination, and utilization management outcomes, while lacking control over payer APIs, 
data quality, benefit determination logic, or implementation timelines. Without explicit 
recognition of this structure, there is a real risk that operational accountability will be misaligned 
with regulatory authority. 
 
This issue is especially significant in CIN and delegated models managing multiple payer 
contracts simultaneously. These organizations must accommodate substantial variability in payer 
implementation maturity, API performance, data requirements, and workflow design for the same 
clinical scenarios. That variability undermines standardization at the network level and creates 
increased denial risk, avoidable rework, training complexity, and administrative burden across 
care teams. 
 
The proposed transition also accelerates the move from legacy HIPAA X12 transactions to API-
based, FHIR-enabled workflows across both medical and pharmacy benefits. Supporting 
multiple standards concurrently, including FHIR Prior Authorization APIs, NCPDP SCRIPT, 
real-time prescription benefit, and formulary standards, will require additional investment in 
integration, monitoring, exception handling, and operational support. These demands are 
heightened in delegated models, where performance expectations may extend across multiple 
parties, but control does not. 
 
CMS should explicitly recognize that accountability frameworks must align with where 
operational control resides. In practice, this means payer-controlled elements such as API 
availability, data quality, endpoint reliability, and transaction performance should be clearly 
reflected within accountability models so that delegated entities can continue to manage 
functions appropriately without assuming disproportionate risk for factors outside their control. 
 
Building Consistent and Integrated Workflows 
Prior authorization for drugs depends on the coordinated exchange of information among a 
variety of entities, including health plans, delegated entities, pharmacies, and pharmacy benefit 
managers. We recommend that CMS account for and support these integrated workflows so 
electronic prior authorization functions as a continuous, end-to-end process. This is essential for 
 
 
1300 S Evergreen Park Dr SW, Suite 200, Olympia, WA 98502 | 360.943.4337 | 1.877.943.4337 | pswipa.com 
achieving a seamless experience for patients, prescribers, care teams, and organizations 
responsible for utilization management and care coordination. 
 
We support expanding NCPDP SCRIPT, formulary and benefit, and real-time prescription 
benefit capabilities beyond Medicare Part D into Medicaid, the Children’s Health Insurance 
Program, and qualified health plans on the federally facilitated exchange. However, CMS should 
require consistent minimum data elements, response behavior, and workflow expectations across 
all lines of business. Without this, organizations operating across contracts will continue to face 
situations where different rules, different data requirements, and different operational pathways 
apply to the same drug, undermining efficiency and equity. 
 
We also support incorporating drugs under the medical benefit into the FHIR-based prior 
authorization API, including computable policy and documentation requirements. However, 
ambiguity between medical and pharmacy benefit pathways remains a significant operational 
risk, particularly for infused drugs, specialty therapies, and other high-cost medications that may 
be adjudicated differently depending on benefit design. Without clearer alignment or 
standardized determination logic, electronic prior authorization could increase misclassification, 
delays, and denial rates rather than reduce administrative burden. 
 
CMS should therefore specify minimum data standards and semantics that support more 
consistent determinations, minimize unnecessary attachments, and improve clarity about the 
applicable benefit pathway. Standards development organizations and FHIR accelerators have 
demonstrated that consensus-driven minimum standards can be established efficiently while 
representing the health ecosystem broadly, and continued reliance on those processes will be 
important here. 
 
Standardized Decision Timeframes 
We support CMS’ proposal to standardize and shorten decision timeframes for prescription 
drugs. However, shorter decision timelines may lead to premature denials, avoidable requests for 
additional information, or perfunctory approvals unless paired with clear, enforceable 
requirements. 
 
To ensure these timelines function as intended, we recommend CMS: 
• Clearly define what constitutes a “completed” request. 
• Allow clinically appropriate extensions when additional documentation is needed. 
• Require denial rationale to be specific, actionable, and traceable to the authorization in 
question. 
• Ensure that timing expectations account for operational dependencies outside the control 
of delegated entities and provider-aligned organizations. 
 
These safeguards will reduce avoidable delays while limiting premature or inappropriate denials. 
 
 
 
 
1300 S Evergreen Park Dr SW, Suite 200, Olympia, WA 98502 | 360.943.4337 | 1.877.943.4337 | pswipa.com 
Implementation Timelines and Reporting 
We are concerned about the aggressive implementation timelines CMS has proposed for 
expanding electronic prior authorization standards. Delegated entities, CINs, and value-based 
organizations will need to support multiple standards concurrently while managing substantial 
variation in payer readiness, performance, and data quality across contracts. We recommend that 
CMS adopt a phased approach to implementation, including safe-harbor periods, to support a 
more stable transition and reduce disruption to care delivery and utilization management 
operations. 
 
We support requiring payers to report interoperability API endpoints and usage metrics. We also 
urge CMS to go further by publishing an authoritative endpoint directory and requiring reporting 
on operational performance metrics, such as availability, latency, and error rates. These steps 
would help ensure that an API not only exists but functions reliably in real-world conditions 
across the full authorization ecosystem. 
 
Conclusion 
 
In closing, as the industry continues moving toward delegated and value-based care models, 
CMS should consider how prior authorization requirements evolve when utilization management 
accountability already exists within a risk-bearing arrangement. In these settings, reduced or 
alternative requirements may be appropriate, provided patient protection and transparency are 
maintained. Aligning policy with these models would better support innovation, reduce 
unnecessary administrative friction, and advance the broader goals of value-based care. 
 
Thank you for considering our comments. We support CMS’ goal to streamline prior 
authorization for prescription drugs and believe the changes outlined above will help ensure 
accountability, reduce misaligned operational burden, and support the delivery of timely, 
equitable, and well-coordinated patient care.  
 
Please let us know if there is additional information we can provide by contacting 
Communications@pswipa.com.   
 
Sincerely, 
PSW & MultiCare Connected Care

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Physicians of Southwest Washington (PSW) and MultiCare Connected Care (MCC).
- **Stakeholder type:** Healthcare Provider; clinically integrated/value-based networks.
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** CINs in Washington State serving over 400,000 individuals across independent practices, health systems, and rural health systems.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

PSW and MCC support electronic prior authorization for drugs but warn that the rule creates near-term operational, technical, and financial risk for delegated, value-based, and health plan-aligned entities. They request phased implementation, standardized payer behavior and data elements, safeguards for shortened decision timeframes, authoritative endpoint reporting, and accountability frameworks that align responsibility with operational control.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING; API-USAGE-METRICS; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS; GENERAL.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** None specifically cited.
- **Standards referenced:** FHIR Prior Authorization APIs; NCPDP SCRIPT; formulary and benefit standards; real-time prescription benefit; legacy HIPAA X12 transactions; standards development organizations and FHIR accelerators.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Electronic prior authorization in delegated models**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Support with modifications
- **Rationale:** Electronic PA can reduce delays and rework, but CINs and delegated entities may be accountable for authorization outcomes without control over payer APIs, benefit logic, data quality, or timelines.
- **Specific request:** Explicitly recognize delegated entities and align accountability with operational control over API reliability, data quality, and transaction performance.

**Topic 2: Concurrent standards and workflow integration**
- **Provision ID:** HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Moving from legacy X12 to FHIR-enabled workflows while also supporting NCPDP standards creates integration, monitoring, and exception-handling burdens.
- **Specific request:** Require end-to-end integrated workflows across payers, delegated entities, pharmacies, PBMs, prescribers, and care teams.

**Topic 3: Standardization across lines of business**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Support/Modify
- **Rationale:** Extending NCPDP capabilities beyond Part D is useful, but inconsistent data requirements and response behaviors will perpetuate multi-payer variation.
- **Specific request:** Require consistent minimum data elements, response behavior, and workflow expectations across Medicaid, CHIP, QHPs, and other covered lines.

**Topic 4: Medical versus pharmacy benefit ambiguity**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL
- **Position:** Clarify
- **Rationale:** Infused drugs, specialty therapies, and high-cost medications may be adjudicated differently depending on benefit design, creating misclassification and denial risk.
- **Specific request:** Specify minimum data standards and semantics for consistent benefit-pathway determinations and computable policy/documentation requirements.

**Topic 5: Decision timeframe safeguards**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Support/Modify
- **Rationale:** Shorter timelines can improve access, but without safeguards may result in premature denials or avoidable additional information requests.
- **Specific request:** Define completed request, allow clinically appropriate extensions, require specific actionable denial rationales, and account for dependencies outside delegated entities' control.

**Topic 6: Implementation timeline and reporting**
- **Provision ID:** API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING; API-USAGE-METRICS; IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Current timelines are aggressive given multi-standard support and payer-readiness variation.
- **Specific request:** Adopt phased implementation and safe-harbor periods; publish an authoritative endpoint directory; require reporting on availability, latency, and error rates.

**Topic 7: Risk-bearing arrangements**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** In value-based and risk-bearing arrangements, utilization management accountability may already exist and duplicative PA can add friction.
- **Specific request:** Allow reduced or alternative PA requirements in risk-bearing models while maintaining patient protections and transparency.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S12:** Supports FHIR-based PA for medical benefit drugs but identifies operational challenges for delegated entities and benefit pathway ambiguity.
- **S14:** Supports expansion of NCPDP SCRIPT/formulary/RTPB capabilities beyond Part D, with consistent minimum requirements across programs.
- **S15:** Responds directly by warning that ambiguity between medical and pharmacy benefit pathways is a major operational risk.
- **S17:** Requests specific, actionable, authorization-traceable denial rationales.
- **S20/S43:** Supports shorter timeframes but asks CMS to define completed requests and permit clinically appropriate extensions.
- **S21:** Raises concern that proposed implementation timelines are aggressive and recommends phased implementation and safe harbors.
- **S23/S24/S26/S27/S33:** Supports endpoint reporting and asks CMS to publish an authoritative endpoint directory with operational performance details.
- **S29/S34/S35:** Supports usage metrics and urges reporting on availability, latency, and error rates.
- **S44-S47:** Addresses transition from X12 to FHIR-enabled workflows and supports a real-world phased transition.
- **S53/S54:** Supports phased implementation, safe harbors, and operational testing/readiness expectations.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Recognize downstream burden on delegated entities, CINs, IPAs, and risk-bearing organizations.
2. Align accountability with operational control over payer APIs and data quality.
3. Require end-to-end integrated prior authorization workflows.
4. Standardize data elements, semantics, response behavior, and workflow expectations across payers and lines of business.
5. Clarify medical versus pharmacy benefit determination logic for specialty and infused drugs.
6. Pair shortened decision timelines with safeguards, completed-request definitions, extensions, and actionable denial rationales.
7. Adopt phased implementation and safe-harbor periods.
8. Publish an authoritative payer endpoint directory.
9. Require operational API metrics including availability, latency, and error rates.
10. Permit evolution or reduction of PA requirements in risk-bearing arrangements.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Misalignment between regulatory accountability and operational control; multi-payer variation; implementation complexity; benefit-pathway ambiguity; aggressive timelines.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Increased denials, rework, training burden, administrative burden, misclassification of drugs, patient delays, and financial risk for delegated organizations.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Payer API variation, data-quality problems, benefit determination logic outside delegated control, concurrent FHIR/NCPDP/X12 support, and differing payer workflows.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** Serves over 400,000 individuals across the Pacific Northwest.
- **Studies or research referenced:** None cited.
- **Examples provided:** Infused drugs, specialty therapies, and high-cost medications may be adjudicated under different benefit pathways depending on plan design.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** CINs, delegated entities, IPAs, risk-bearing organizations, providers, care teams, patients, payers, pharmacies, and PBMs.
- **Economic implications:** Requires investment in integration, monitoring, exception handling, training, and operational support.
- **Technical feasibility:** Feasible if phased and standardized; risky if payer variability and API performance are unmanaged.
- **Patient care impact:** Well-implemented ePA may speed access to high-cost therapies; poorly implemented requirements could increase denials and delays.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Mixed/supportive with significant implementation concerns
- **Tone:** Collaborative, operational, and technical
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "We support this rule and agree that it has the potential to reduce administrative burden over time and improve patient access to needed therapies." - Context: Overall position.
2. "There is a real risk that operational accountability will be misaligned with regulatory authority." - Context: Delegated model concern.
3. "Ambiguity between medical and pharmacy benefit pathways remains a significant operational risk." - Context: Specialty and infused drug classification.
4. "We recommend that CMS adopt a phased approach to implementation, including safe-harbor periods." - Context: Implementation timeline recommendation.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - The comment asks for phased implementation and safe harbors.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - Delegated entities must invest in integration, monitoring, exception handling, and training.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Multi-payer variation creates rework and administrative burden for care teams.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - API performance, data quality, and concurrent standards support are central concerns.
- [x] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - The comment discusses FHIR, NCPDP, X12 transition, and standards development processes.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - ePA could improve access, but poor implementation could increase delays and denials.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - Requires coordination among payers, delegated entities, pharmacies, PBMs, prescribers, and care teams.
- [x] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** - The comment specifically calls out ambiguity between benefit pathways.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Requests actionable denial rationales, endpoint directory, and operational metrics.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Focuses on real-world delegated and value-based care workflows.
